name: Doha
tagline: Gulf capital of bold museums and desert sea.
bestMonths: Jan, Feb, Mar, Apr, Nov and Dec
whenBlurb: November to March is the only real window, warm days for the corniche, museums and desert; the jewellery and film weeks and National Day cluster here, and summer is best avoided entirely.

ourTake.lede: Doha has become a genuinely serious cultural stop, not just a stopover. Give it two full days: the Museum of Islamic Art is world-class, and the restored Msheireb quarter and the Souq Waqif are best walked in the evening cool. Time a visit around National Day if you can, the waterfront comes alive.
ourTake.comeIf: You want a compact, refined Gulf stay built around world-class museums and a short, easy flight.
ourTake.skipIf: You want a week of variety; Doha rewards a focused few days more than a long stay.

guide.lede: Where to stay, what to do, where to eat, and where the night goes, grouped by price, every address earned by a name worth trusting.

items.name: Mandarin Oriental, Doha
credentials: Forbes Travel Guide 5-Star (2025, sixth consecutive year)
items.description: The group's quiet precision, dropped into the restored heart of the old city.

items.name: Four Seasons Hotel Doha
items.description: The surest hands in the city, service you never have to think about, on its own beach.

items.name: Raffles Doha
items.description: Qatar's first all-suite house, inside the crossed-sabre towers, theatre with Raffles butlers.

items.name: Rosewood Doha
items.description: A soaring twin-tower newcomer that took a Forbes Five-Star in its first year.

items.name: Four Seasons Resort and Residences at The Pearl-Qatar
items.description: A marina-side resort address on the man-made island, with Four Seasons ease throughout.

items.name: Sharq Village & Spa, a Ritz-Carlton Hotel
items.description: A low-slung Qatari 'village' by the sea, the calm, traditional counterpoint to the towers.

items.name: The Chedi Katara Hotel & Resort, Doha
items.description: GHM's understated design ideal beside the cultural village and its private beach.

items.name: The Ritz-Carlton, Doha
items.description: A grand marina resort with its own beach and yacht berths, classic Ritz-Carlton scale.

items.name: The St. Regis Doha
items.description: A palatial Gulf-front retreat with the signature St. Regis butler on every floor.

items.name: Waldorf Astoria Doha Lusail
items.description: New-city grandeur on the Lusail waterfront, polished, spacious, of the moment.

items.name: Marsa Malaz Kempinski, The Pearl-Doha
items.description: A palace-scaled island house at the gateway to The Pearl, unabashedly grand.

items.name: Fairmont Doha
items.description: The second of the crossed-sabre towers, gold-leaf glamour on a grand scale.

items.name: The Ned Doha
items.description: A landmark government building reborn as a members'-club-and-hotel with real buzz.

items.name: Mondrian Doha
items.description: Maximalist, design-forward drama for the member who wants the volume turned up.

items.name: W Doha
items.description: A high-energy design house in the business district, for celebrations, not quiet nights.

items.name: Banyan Tree Doha
items.description: A spa-led vertical retreat with a sky-high pool over the downtown skyline.

items.name: Banana Island Resort Doha by Anantara
items.description: A ferry-only island escape with over-water villas, the closest thing to a beach holiday off Doha.

items.name: The Plaza Doha, LXR Hotels & Resorts
items.description: A jewel-box LXR house in the walkable downtown quarter, all quiet polish.

items.name: InterContinental Doha Beach & Spa
items.description: A long-established beach resort with the city's largest private stretch of sand.

items.name: Waldorf Astoria Doha West Bay
items.description: A polished business-district tower with Waldorf Astoria service at a gentler price.

items.name: Museum of Islamic Art
credentials: Designed by I.M. Pei, his final museum commission
items.description: I.M. Pei's last great building rises out of the bay like a stack of cubes, holding one of the world's finest collections of Islamic art across three continents and 1,400 years. A private curator-led morning suits multi-generational families, and the fifth-floor IDAM restaurant makes an unhurried lunch with skyline views.

items.name: National Museum of Qatar
items.description: Jean Nouvel's 'desert rose' of 600 interlocking sand-coloured discs wraps around the restored 20th-century royal palace, telling Qatar's story through vast 360-degree film galleries. It is visual, walkable and captivating for children and grandparents alike, and the on-site Jiwan restaurant does an elegant Qatari tasting menu.

items.name: Souq Waqif
items.description: The beating heart of old Doha, restored mud-rendered lanes of spice stalls, oud perfumers, textile and gold merchants, and open-air cafes where families linger over mint tea and shisha. A private guide can time an evening visit around the cooler air and steer you to the best vegetarian mezze houses.

items.name: Katara Cultural Village
items.description: A purpose-built seafront village of galleries, an open-air amphitheatre for 5,000, and two jewel-box mosques, the blue-tiled Katara Mosque and the shimmering Golden Mosque. Free to enter, easy to wander, and lined with restaurants that make it a relaxed multi-generational half-day.

items.name: The Pearl-Qatar
items.description: A man-made island of Riviera-style marinas, superyachts and flagship boutiques, with the Venice-inspired Qanat Quartier and its pastel canals. Ideal for an evening stroll, waterfront dining and discreet luxury shopping, with the Marsa Malaz Kempinski palace hotel anchoring one end.

items.name: Msheireb Downtown Doha
items.description: One of the world's first smart, sustainable regenerated city centres, cool pale-stone streets, wind-tower shade and contemporary Qatari architecture, walking distance from Souq Waqif. A calm, cerebral counterpoint to the souq for slower afternoons.

items.name: Msheireb Museums
items.description: Four restored 1900s heritage houses, Bin Jelmood, Company House, Mohammed Bin Jassim and Radwani, trace Qatar's oil story, community life and a candid history of slavery in the Gulf. Thoughtful, air-conditioned and free, and a meaningful stop for older children and grandparents.

items.name: Doha Corniche
items.description: A seven-kilometre crescent promenade curving around the bay, framing the West Bay skyline on one side and traditional dhows on the other. Best walked at dusk or early morning; a private car can drop and collect at either end for older travellers.

items.name: West Bay skyline & viewpoints
items.description: Doha's cluster of futuristic towers, the twisting Tornado Tower, the Doha Tower and their neighbours, is the postcard image of the city, best seen from a dhow on the bay or a high sky-bar at golden hour. A discreet way to bookend a day of culture with a drink and a view.

items.name: MIA Park & '7' by Richard Serra
credentials: '7', Richard Serra's tallest sculpture and first public work in the Middle East
items.description: The landscaped park behind the Museum of Islamic Art runs out to a 24-metre steel monument by Richard Serra, his tallest work and first public sculpture in the Middle East, echoing the number seven's meaning in Islam. Space for children to run and one of the finest skyline photo spots in Doha.

items.name: Mathaf: Arab Museum of Modern Art
credentials: World's largest collection of modern and contemporary Arab art
items.description: The world's largest collection of modern and contemporary Arab art, over 9,000 works from the 1840s to today, housed in a converted school in Education City. A serious, quieter museum for guests who want depth beyond the headline icons.

items.name: 3-2-1 Qatar Olympic and Sports Museum
items.description: A vivid, interactive sports museum shaped like the five Olympic rings, tracing global sporting history alongside Qatar's own. Hands-on challenges and simulators make it a genuine hit with children and teenagers.

items.name: Falcon Souq
items.description: A dedicated corner of Souq Waqif where prized hunting falcons perch hooded on gloved stands and are traded for eye-watering sums, a living window into Qatari heritage. Guides can arrange a respectful, unhurried visit that fascinates all ages.

items.name: Souq Waqif Falcon Hospital
items.description: A state-of-the-art three-storey hospital, subsidised by the Emir, that treats up to 150 birds a day in falconry season, from chipped talons to feather transplants. An unexpected, memorable stop that a private guide can slot in beside the Falcon Souq.

items.name: Qatar National Library
items.description: Rem Koolhaas's angular concrete-and-glass hall folds down into a sunken travertine 'heritage' pit holding 4,000 rare manuscripts and a 1478 Ptolemaic map. A design pilgrimage for the architecturally curious, and a serene, cool space to pause.

items.name: Dhow cruise on Doha Bay
items.description: A traditional wooden dhow gliding across the bay is the classic way to take in the West Bay skyline, day or night. Charter one privately for the family, with a table set for a sunset meal and the option to keep it fully vegetarian.

items.name: Khor Al Adaid (the Inland Sea)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Tentative List, Khor Al-Adaid Natural Reserve
items.description: A UNESCO-tentative natural reserve where towering dunes tumble straight into a tidal sea lagoon, one of very few places on earth this happens. Reachable only by 4x4 with an expert driver; a private convoy with a chef-catered majlis camp turns it into an unforgettable desert day.

items.name: Sealine desert & dunes
items.description: Under an hour south of Doha, the Sealine dunes are the launch point for dune bashing, sandboarding, quad biking and camel rides across rolling golden sand. A private guide can tailor the intensity, gentle camel rides for grandparents, adrenaline runs for teenagers.

items.name: Al Zubarah Archaeological Site
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Al Zubarah Archaeological Site
items.description: Roughly 105 km northwest of Doha, this walled 18th-19th-century pearling and trading town is the best-preserved of its kind in the Gulf, paired with a handsome restored fort. A rewarding half-day drive for history-minded families with a knowledgeable guide.

items.name: Aspire Park & the Torch
items.description: Doha's largest park, 88 hectares of lawns, a lake and shaded walks, sits beneath the 300-metre Torch tower with its revolving restaurant and vertiginous observation deck. Green space for children by day, skyline dining by night.

items.name: Villaggio Mall
items.description: A Venetian-themed mall with a painted-sky ceiling and real gondola rides along an indoor canal, packed with luxury and family brands and connected to the Torch by covered walkway. A cool, playful afternoon that keeps children entertained while adults shop.

items.name: Place Vendôme Mall
credentials: Home to the largest Louis Vuitton store in the Middle East
items.description: A $1.3bn French-classical mega-mall in Lusail, home to the Middle East's largest Louis Vuitton, flagship Cartier and Bvlgari, and an hourly dancing-fountain show over a 7,400 sqm canal. The pinnacle of discreet Doha luxury shopping and evening dining.

items.name: Banana Island Resort by Anantara
items.description: A crescent-shaped private island a 30-minute catamaran ride from the city, with a long private beach, over-water villas, a surf pool, bowling and cinema, and it is entirely alcohol-free. A day pass or overnight makes a serene multi-generational escape.

items.name: Camel racing at Al Shahaniya
items.description: About an hour from Doha, thoroughbred racing camels thunder down the track steered by robot jockeys while owners follow in 4x4s alongside, a genuinely surreal Qatari spectacle. Early-morning training runs are the atmospheric time to watch with a guide.

items.name: Sheikh Faisal Bin Qassim Al Thani Museum
items.description: A private collector's 'cabinet of curiosities' of over 30,000 objects, from Jurassic fossils and Islamic art to vintage cars and the world's largest private sword collection. Endlessly surprising, and a favourite of curious children on the drive out to the desert.

items.name: Katara Towers (Raffles & Fairmont)
items.description: The crescent-shaped twin towers, modelled on the crossed sabres of Qatar's coat of arms, house the Raffles and Fairmont hotels and the city's largest ballroom. Even for non-guests it is a striking architectural stop and a polished spot for afternoon tea.

items.name: Lusail Boulevard & Marina
items.description: Qatar's 'city of the future' laid out along a grand pedestrian boulevard of cafes, boutiques and seasonal drone light shows, running down to a yacht-lined marina promenade. A relaxed evening for families once the desert heat lifts.

items.name: Al Wakrah Souq & dhow harbour
items.description: A beautifully restored fishing-village souq south of Doha, with its own beach, boutique heritage hotels and a harbour full of traditional dhows. Quieter and more atmospheric than the main souq, lovely for an unhurried lunch by the water.

items.name: Purple Island (Bin Ghannam) mangroves
items.description: A peaceful peninsula near Al Khor named for its ancient purple-dye industry, threaded with mangrove creeks best explored by kayak among wading birds. A gentle nature outing that guides can arrange with stable double kayaks for mixed-ability groups.

items.name: Barzan Towers
items.description: A pair of restored late-19th-century watchtowers about 15 km north of Doha, once used to guard water and to sight the moon for the Islamic calendar. A quick, free, atmospheric stop that pairs well with a northern day-trip.

items.name: Fire Station: Artists in Residence
items.description: A former civil-defence fire station near central Doha reborn as a contemporary art complex, studios, changing exhibitions, a cinema and a well-regarded cafe. A cool, low-key stop for guests who like their culture current rather than curated.

items.name: Al Thuraya Planetarium
items.description: A modern planetarium within Katara Cultural Village blending astronomy with the history of Arab celestial navigation under a full-dome sky. A charming, air-conditioned option that delights younger children on a Katara afternoon.

items.name: Al Bidda Park
items.description: A large, gently landscaped park hugging the Corniche with shaded walks, play areas and easy skyline views. A convenient green breather between the museums and the waterfront for families with small children.

items.name: Aspire Zone & Khalifa International Stadium
items.description: Qatar's flagship sports precinct, home to the historic Khalifa International Stadium and world-class facilities from the 2022 World Cup era. Stadium tours and the surrounding parkland make an easy outing for sport-minded travellers and teenagers.

items.name: Galeries Lafayette Doha (Katara Plaza)
items.description: The French department-store landmark reimagined at Katara, gathering luxury fashion, beauty and a gourmet food hall under one elegant roof. A refined, unhurried shopping stop steps from the cultural village.

items.name: Gold Souq
items.description: A dedicated lane within the souq district where cases glitter with 21- and 22-karat gold and intricate Gulf jewellery, prices set largely by weight. A guide who knows the trusted merchants makes buying, or simply marvelling, a comfortable experience.

items.name: Doha Oyster & Pearl Monument
items.description: The much-photographed sculpture of an oyster cradling a giant pearl, honouring Qatar's pre-oil pearling heritage on the West Bay waterfront. A quick, iconic photo stop woven into a Corniche drive.

items.name: Doha Metro (Msheireb station)
items.description: A driverless, marble-and-vaulted metro that is a design attraction in its own right, with Msheireb the palatial central interchange. A cool, novel way to hop between museums and Education City that even luxury travellers enjoy for a stop or two.

items.name: Qatar National Convention Centre (Sidra Tree)
items.description: A dramatic Arata Isozaki building whose facade branches like the sidra tree that shelters poets and scholars in Qatari lore. Worth a photo pass on any Education City visit for the architecture alone.

items.name: Education City public art & mosque
credentials: Features Damien Hirst's 'The Miraculous Journey' sculptures
items.description: The Qatar Foundation campus doubles as an open-air gallery, Damien Hirst's monumental 'Miraculous Journey' bronzes outside Sidra Medicine and the striking calligraphy-clad Education City Mosque. A quiet, cultured drive-through with a knowledgeable guide.

items.name: Souq Al Wakra beach & heritage hotels
items.description: The restored waterfront at Al Wakra pairs a golden public beach with boutique heritage stays built into the old souq's coral-stone houses. A restful seaside afternoon away from the city's pace, easily private-guided.

items.name: Doha's public art trail
items.description: Beyond Serra's '7', Doha has seeded world-class art across the city, from airport and Hamad hospital commissions to sculptures dotting parks and roundabouts. A curator-led art drive stitches the highlights into a single, cultured half-day.

items.name: Katara Beach & Katara Hills
items.description: A 1.5-kilometre family-friendly beach with watersports and parasailing sits beside the cultural village, backed by the twin Katara Hills for sea views. An easy way to add a little sun and sand to a culture-heavy Katara day.

items.name: IDAM by Alain Ducasse
credentials: MENA's 50 Best #44 (2026, Best Restaurant in Qatar)
items.description: Ducasse's French-Mediterranean, on the museum's top floor, with Doha Bay filling the glass.

items.name: Alba
items.description: Piedmontese cooking of real refinement inside the crossed-sabre towers, Doha's newest star.

items.name: Nobu Doha
items.area: Four Seasons Hotel Doha, West Bay
items.description: The largest Nobu in the world, floating over the Gulf, the black cod that conquered the planet.

items.name: Carbone Doha
items.description: The New York Italian-American theatre, tableside Caesar, veal parm and red sauce, done grandly.

items.name: Curiosa by Jean-Georges
items.description: Jean-Georges Vongerichten's playful, produce-led cooking in a jewel-box island room.

items.name: Jamavar
items.description: The Leela's grand pan-Indian house, the first Indian restaurant to win a Doha star.

items.name: Jiwan
items.description: Modern Qatari cooking under the museum's desert-rose roof, heritage, elevated.

items.name: Zuma Doha
items.description: The izakaya benchmark that never empties, precise, buzzy, endlessly reliable.

items.name: Hakkasan Doha
items.description: The Cantonese standard-bearer, dim sum and lacquered duck in a low-lit lattice room.

items.name: Morimoto Doha
items.description: Iron Chef Masaharu Morimoto's Japanese, staged with Mondrian theatre.

items.name: COYA Doha
items.description: Peruvian colour and pisco energy, ceviche, anticuchos and a room that never quiets.

items.name: La Mar Doha by Gastón Acurio
items.area: InterContinental Doha Beach & Spa, West Bay
items.description: Gastón Acurio's seaside Peruvian, bright cebiches and a long beachfront terrace.

items.name: La Petite Maison (LPM) Doha
items.description: Riviera cooking and a room that has never gone out of fashion, the Niçoise classic.

items.name: Gymkhana Doha
items.description: The Sethi family's colonial-club Indian, smoke, spice and swagger, carried from Mayfair.

items.name: Masala Library Doha
items.description: Jiggs Kalra's progressive Indian, familiar flavours, reimagined with a light modern hand.

items.name: Em Sherif Doha
items.description: Beirut's grand Lebanese table, an endless, generous procession of mezze.

items.name: Shanghai Me Doha
items.description: 1930s-Shanghai glamour and pan-Asian cooking with real intent.

items.name: Hoppers
items.description: Sri Lankan and South Indian home cooking, hoppers, kari and roti done with real soul.

items.name: Isaan
items.description: Northeastern Thai cooking with genuine fire and fragrance, a Bib-listed favourite.

items.name: Argan
items.description: Generous, aromatic Moroccan cooking, tagines and pastilla with a proper hand.

items.name: Mila
items.description: Bright Mediterranean and Levantine sharing plates in the Rosewood's newest room.

items.name: Berenjak Al Maha Island
items.description: Tehran's back-street kebab houses recreated over coals, hearty, smoky, generous.

items.name: Baron
items.description: Characterful, generous Mediterranean cooking, a Beirut name that earned its Bib in Doha.

items.name: Dalchini
items.description: Indian-Chinese and pan-Asian comfort cooking with a devoted local following.

items.name: Dar Yema
items.description: Qatari home cooking preserved and served with pride, a rare taste of the real thing.

items.name: Fenyal
items.description: Vibrant, pocket-friendly Khaleeji cooking, falafel, lamb kofta and proper Arabic coffee.

items.name: The lounge bar at Rosewood Doha
credentials: Within Rosewood Doha (Forbes 5-Star, MICHELIN One Key)
items.description: A polished sky-lounge in the twin-tower newcomer that took a Forbes Five-Star in its first year, a smart, contemporary place to begin the evening.

items.name: Ambar, Mandarin Oriental
credentials: Within Mandarin Oriental, Doha (Forbes 5-Star, MICHELIN One Key)
items.description: The quietly assured lounge in the group's Msheireb house, considered cocktails and artisanal bites, in the calmest, most central address in the city.

items.name: Nobu Doha rooftop lounge
credentials: Within Four Seasons Hotel Doha (Forbes 5-Star, MICHELIN One Key)
items.description: The bar level of the largest Nobu in the world, a three-storey pavilion over the Gulf, cocktails and tapas with the West Bay skyline in the glass.

items.name: The rooftop bar at Raffles Doha
credentials: Within Raffles Doha (Forbes 5-Star, MICHELIN Two Keys)
items.description: Live soul and jazz and 360-degree views from inside the crossed-sabre towers, the highest, most theatrical drink in the new city.

plan.heading: 3 days in Doha, done well
plan.lede: A day-by-day shape for the trip, the pace we would set. Your advisor books the flights and the rooms; the days are yours.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Walk I.M. Pei's Museum of Islamic Art at opening, then the sculpture park on the water.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Check into the Mandarin Oriental in Msheireb, lunch, then the restored lanes of Msheireb Downtown.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at IDAM, Alain Ducasse's room atop the Museum of Islamic Art, with the skyline across the bay.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Coffee and the falcon souq at Souq Waqif while the morning is cool.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Drive south to the Khor Al Adaid inland sea, where the dunes meet the Gulf, with a private guide.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Return for dinner at Jiwan by Alain Ducasse at the National Museum of Qatar, Jean Nouvel's desert-rose building.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: The collections at Mathaf and the National Museum of Qatar, then the boutiques of Place Vendôme.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: A dhow out to the old pearl banks off Al Wakrah, lunch aboard.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: A farewell dinner at Toro Toro, then drinks high over West Bay.

items.name: West Bay
items.description: For skyline hotels and the corporate polish; convenient but glassy and car-dependent.

items.name: Msheireb Downtown
items.description: For the walkable, restored heart of old Doha, low-rise, cultured, and near the souq.

items.name: The Pearl
items.description: For marina living, waterfront dining and a resort feel a short drive from the centre.

events.name: Qatar National Day
events.note: A waterfront parade, air and sea displays and fireworks marking the country's unification.

events.name: Ajyal Film Festival
events.note: The Doha Film Institute's week-long festival at Katara, screenings and culture for all ages.

onGround.heading: On the ground
onGround.note: The Pearl and West Bay are the polished places to stay; Qatar is more conservative than the UAE, so dress modestly in public, and alcohol is confined to licensed hotel venues. The National Museum and Museum of Islamic Art are unmissable and never crowded.

rows.label: Arriving
rows.value: Land at Hamad International (DOH), consistently rated among the world's finest airports, where Al Maha meet-and-assist walks you through immigration to a waiting chauffeured car for the short run into the city.

rows.label: Getting around
rows.value: A private car covers the distances; the Corniche, Msheireb and Souq Waqif are best explored on foot, and a traditional dhow makes an elegant way to see the West Bay skyline from the water.

rows.label: Connectivity
rows.value: An eSIM from Ooredoo or Vodafone Qatar gives fast 5G on arrival; wifi is excellent throughout hotels and the airport.

rows.label: Money
rows.value: The Qatari riyal (QAR), pegged to the dollar; cards are standard, cash is handy in the souq, and tipping is appreciated but not expected as service charges apply.

rows.label: Climate
rows.value: November to March is the kind season: mild 22-27C days, clear skies for the Corniche and desert. Avoid June-September, when heat exceeds 42C with heavy humidity off the Gulf.

rows.label: Flights from India
rows.value: Direct from Delhi, Mumbai and Bengaluru, roughly 4 hours. Qatar Airways flies it best; its Qsuite business product is class-leading, with first-class comfort in a business cabin. Al Mourjan and the Al Safwa first lounge at Hamad International are outstanding for onward connections across Qatar's global network.

rows.label: Health & safety
rows.value: No vaccinations required beyond routine; hepatitis A and typhoid advisable. Extremely safe and orderly. Tap water is desalinated and safe, bottled is customary. Summer heat is the main concern.

rows.label: Dining, veg & Jain
rows.value: Straightforward for vegetarian and Jain travellers. Indian cuisine is abundant and pure-veg is easily arranged. Saffron Lounge and the Indian kitchens across West Bay are dependable; luxury hotels handle Jain requirements on notice.
